newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean union groups vow to step up action.
newsitem.headline: South Korean union groups vow to step up action.

text.p: South Korea's two union umbrella groups said on Saturday they would step up industrial action in the coming week to back their demand for the withdrawal of a controversial labour law.
"Strikes will escalate until the government repeals the revised labour law," Kwon Young-kil, chairman of the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions, told reporters.
"The government will see the graveness of the situation next week," he added.
Kwon said about 200 unions at the nation's major car makers, ship builders, other manufacturers and secondary financial institutions, comprising 230,000 members, would go strike from Monday morning.

"From Tuesday, unionised workers at subway, hospitals and broadcasting companies will join in the work stoppage. We have also proposed to cooperate with the Federation of Korean Trade Unions," Kwon said.
The two umbrella union groups claim an aggregate 1.7 million members in most of South Korea's major industries and public-sector services.

Nation-wide strikes erupted on December 26 after the ruling New Korea Party pushed through a new labour during a clandestine session of parliament. The law gives employers the right to lay off employees, hire temporary workers and replace strikers.
The work stoppages, which hit car and ship production, hospitals and subways, were postponed until after the New Year holidays to spare the public.
The government has said changes in the law would benefit unions and employers by creating a more flexible labour market.
Last Friday a strike call by the Korea Confederation of Trade Unions received a mixed response.
The body said about 96,000 workers at 46 unions answered its call, while the Labour Ministry put its estimate at 22,884 workers of 31 unions.
Kwon accused the government of scaling down the numbers and plotting to "paint the confederation as backing down".
The number of striking workers dropped in half on Saturday because many companies extended the New Year holidays until Sunday, the confederation said.
Fears of labour unrest continued to hurt the nation's stock market, with the Seoul bourse falling to a 45-month low by the end of the Saturday's half-day session.
The composite index fell 10.38 points to 643.41, the lowest since March 16, 1993, when it ended at 637.87.
"Labour unrest is expected to flare up again from Monday. That expectation prompted sales of shares," said Kim Heung-shik, a broker at Hyundai Securities.

The unrest would intensify in the coming week because the more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the nation's largest union group, was already organising large-scale anti-government rallies.
The federation earlier said it planned a large-scale rally on January 10 and a general strike by all of its members was postponed until January 11.
"We will organise rallies in Seoul, Inchon, Pusan and other cities from Saturday to push our demand for the cancellation of the law," the federation said in a statement.
The body said its second round of strikes would be led by unions in the public and service sectors.
"I hope the government does not underestimate our will to fight," said a federation spokesman.
